title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication is missing or invalid
description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) (and other exceptions), clears g.user, and then still invokes the protected handler. Any protected handler that does not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be reached without authentication, while others produce an avoidable 500 instead of a 401.
evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned the complete order JSON with HTTP 200. The wrapper catches abort(401) at line 54 and calls the endpoint at shopapi/orders.py:46-50, which uses get_order() but never verifies ownership.

title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and only checks that the subject maps to a user. An attacker can create an unsigned token naming any user and obtain a valid signed session token for that account.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT whose payload was {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a fresh HS256 token for user 1. No signature or expiration validation is performed before load_user().

title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
description: The global admin check compares request.path to the set of exact route rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ is a valid route but is not equal to the collected /admin/refunds rule; unauthenticated callers can execute the refund operation.
evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header and body {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. The authorization hook is at shopapi/__init__.py:35-41 and only checks exact request.path membership.

title: Authenticated users can read other customers' orders
description: show_order calls get_order rather than own_order, so any authenticated user (and, due to the decorator bug, even an unauthenticated request) can retrieve another customer's order, item and refund details.
evidence: GET /orders/1 without credentials returned order 1, including its items, payment totals and refund history. The ownership check exists in own_order() at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order().

title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
description: The q parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being bound as a parameter. This permits modification of the query and potentially broader database access through SQLite SQL injection techniques.
evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, demonstrating that the input changed the WHERE predicate.

title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as trusted HTML
description: Review body input is stored without sanitization and the product template renders r.body with the safe filter. A logged-in user can persist arbitrary HTML/script markup that executes for anyone viewing the product page.
evidence: POST /products/<product_id>/reviews accepts body without bleach.clean(), and shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. This is a stored XSS path from the review API to every product-page visitor.

title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
description: For every request with an Origin header, the application reflects that origin and enables credentialed CORS. Any hostile website can therefore make credentialed cross-origin requests if the browser has usable authentication state, and the application provides no allowlist.
evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. config.py:12 enables CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS globally.

title: JWT and webhook signing secret is hardcoded in source
description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed repository value rather than a required deployment secret. Anyone who obtains the source or reads this value can forge HS256 authentication tokens and, because the webhook uses the same application configuration family of secrets, the deployment's trust boundary is compromised. The default WEBHOOK_SECRET is also predictable at line 8.
evidence: config.py:3 contains SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to "whsec-local". JWT signing uses SECRET_KEY at shopapi/auth.py:27 and webhook verification uses WEBHOOK_SECRET at shopapi/payments.py:53-64.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashing uses a single fast SHA-256 digest with no salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking and makes equal passwords identifiable; a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt should be used.
evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and the resulting value is stored directly in users.password_hash by registration and reset flows.

title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks orders paid
description: When the payment provider times out, the exception handler sets status to paid instead of leaving the order awaiting payment or requiring reconciliation. A provider outage or induced timeout can therefore cause goods to be dispatched without confirmed payment.
evidence: shopapi/payments.py:39-44 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = "paid", and then updates the order to processing with paid_pence = total_pence.

title: Payment webhook does not validate the paid amount
description: The webhook authenticates only order_id via its signature and accepts any supplied amount_pence, including zero or an amount below the order total, while transitioning the order to processing. A sender possessing the webhook secret can underpay an order, and the application does not enforce the invariant that paid_pence covers total_pence.
evidence: The paid branch at lines 69-71 casts event.amount_pence and writes it directly to paid_pence without comparing it with order.total_pence. The signature at lines 53-55 covers only order_id, not status or amount.

title: Request logger records sensitive request bodies
description: All POST, PUT and PATCH bodies are written to application logs, including login passwords, password reset codes, bearer-like secrets submitted in JSON, payment data supplied by clients, and personal information. Logs commonly have broader retention and access than the application and this creates unnecessary credential and privacy exposure.
evidence: before_request log_request() calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every mutating request at lines 30-31; /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm send passwords and reset codes in those bodies.

title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
description: The runnable application starts Flask with debug=True. If this entry point is used in a reachable deployment, unhandled exceptions expose interactive debugger functionality and detailed internals; debug mode must not be enabled for production serving.
evidence: run.py:6 calls app.run(..., debug=True). The live app also returned an HTML 500 response for an exception path, demonstrating that this executable is an active deployment entry point.
